statements.venue: Video released by his Senate office, quoted in a press release
statements.quote: If America wants to lead the world in energy, manufacturing, and artificial intelligence, we need to be able to actually build things again.
statements.context: He was arguing for faster federal permitting of energy and infrastructure projects.
statements.reason: Promotes American leadership in AI and does not mention any risk from AI.

statements.source_label: Senate site repost of 535 News op-ed

record: Not among the 17 signers of the 23 September 2026 letter urging AI talks with China (all signers were Democrats).
Introduced the American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure Act (permitting reform; AI appears only as a source of power demand).
grade_reason: Every AI remark found treats AI as an economic and energy-demand matter tied to permitting reform and data centers. Nothing found acknowledges, or dismisses, catastrophic risk from AI.
notes: Six web searches ran, none refused. The searches on superintelligence, extinction, pause, China agreement and AI safety returned nothing mentioning Armstrong. Four armstrong.senate.gov pages were then downloaded directly and read, plus the site's own search for 'artificial intelligence' and its business issues page (data centers, Tulsa applied AI cluster; all promotional). Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act: no source found showing him as a co-sponsor; I did not check the bill's co-sponsor list on congress.gov, so this is 'no evidence', not a verified 'no'. Left out: a Columbia Energy Exchange podcast summary on his site (2026-07-31, https://www.armstrong.senate.gov/senator-alan-armstrong-outlines-country-first-energy-principles-and-urgent-need-for-permitting-reform-on-columbia-energy-exchange-podcast/) quotes him saying slow permitting 'should scare us as Americans when we're in a race right now to be able to have the best computing power in the world'; the office's version has an ellipsis and is about competition, so it would be D and was not used as a quote. Dates: the 535 News op-ed date is the date of the Senate site repost; the original publication may be a few days earlier. The Tulsa World op-ed date is as shown on the Senate site (the page URL says 'Oklahoman' but the byline says Tulsa World).
